Hooded siskins (Spinus magellanicus) are small-bodied cardueline finches whose life-history traits reflect their neotropical distribution. For their body size, they exhibit a moderate metabolic rate; basal oxygen consumption has been measured at 36.36 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 36.36 milliliters of oxygen per hour] under standard thermoneutral conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a value consistent with that of other granivorous passerines in the Thraupidae family. At birth, nestlings emerge from the egg at a wet mass of 1.39 grams [Wwb = 1.39 grams], a modest mass typical of altricial young. This initial weight increases rapidly as the developing chick is brooded over an incubation period of 13 days [ab = 13 days] at 34 °C [T = 34 °C], a figure corroborated by field data from congeneric species. Following hatching, the nestling period proceeds under intense parental provisioning.

After hatching, the nestling enters a phase of rapid somatic growth toward the adult body mass. Adult females ultimately attain an asymptotic body mass of 13.6 grams [Wwi = 13.6 grams], a dimension that places the hooded siskin among the smaller members of its genus. This ultimate wet weight is achieved during the post-juvenile molt and is sustained throughout the breeding season, reflecting the energetic demands of egg production. At the standard thermoneutral temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the progression of life-history stages is well-defined: fledging, which signals flight capability and early independence, occurs at 19 days after hatching [tx = 19 days after hatching], aligning with the documented range of 18 to 21 days. Nestlings that reach this milestone are then classified as fledglings, transitioning to a juvenile stage of development.

Sexual maturation in the hooded siskin follows a well-defined timetable. Pubertal development under 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] is achieved at 57 days after hatching [tp = 57 days after hatching], marking the onset of gonadal activity and the development of secondary sexual characteristics, particularly the black cap and bib in males. The relatively rapid progression for a passerine of this body size is somewhat shorter than that observed in several larger neotropical finches, a pattern that aligns with the general allometric scaling of reproductive development among birds. The timing of puberty is ultimately constrained by the achievement of adult body mass, as individuals must first complete their somatic growth before diverting resources toward gamete production.

Reproduction in the hooded siskin is characterized by serial polygyny and high annual output. In their native range, females typically lay 3 to 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3 to 5 eggs per clutch] and can complete between 2 and 4 nesting attempts annually [F_R_i = between 2 and 4 nesting attempts annually], a strategy that maximizes lifetime fecundity in response to seasonal resource pulses. The first successful reproductive event occurs at one year since birth [tR = one year since birth], a figure recorded under the standard thermoneutral conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This age at first brood represents a conservative life history adapted to the variable seed availability of their subtropical habitats. The combination of moderate clutch sizes with multiple broods per year yields a substantial annual reproductive potential that buffers populations against years of poor food availability and high nest predation rates, common pressures in their native scrub and open woodland environments.

Longevity in the hooded siskin is modest compared to larger passerines, consistent with its small body size and fast life-history pace. Maximum recorded lifespan under natural conditions reaches 9.3 years [am = 9.3 years] when measured at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a value consistent with the short-lived, high-fecundity strategy typical of small granivorous passerines. This figure, equivalent to approximately 3395 days, has been documented from banding returns and represents the upper bound of survival in the wild. In captivity, individuals may exceed this duration, with some records approaching 12 years, though such extremes are rarely achieved in the field owing to predation, disease, and resource limitation. This life-history strategy is typical of many small-bodied granivorous birds that rely on high turnover rates to maintain stable population densities.
